issues.legal_issue: An eviction direction under the emergency rule is invalid when it is issued by an official who lacks authority to exercise the power assigned to the central government.
material_facts: The challenged direction ordered the occupants of public premises to vacate under Rule 155 of the Defence of India Rules.
The direction was issued by a deputy secretary who, as was conceded, had no authority under the Rules of Business to exercise the central government’s powers.
Rule 155 assigned the power to make an eviction order to the central government.
issues.conclusion: The direction was wholly illegal, ineffective and void, and the appeal was allowed and the direction set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 155(1) of the Defence of India Rules empowered the central government to make the eviction order and required strict compliance with the rule. Under Rules 3 and 11 of the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961, the relevant business was to be disposed of by or under the directions of the minister in charge, and the department’s secretary was responsible for its proper transaction. An official could issue the order only if duly empowered to act for the central government. The Court assumed the validity of Rule 155 and relied on no earlier cases.

predicates.challenge_to_public_premises_eviction_or: The proceeding challenges an order directing occupants to vacate public premises under an emergency rule.
predicates.order_issued_by_unempowered_official: An official without authority to act for the central government issued the eviction direction, although the rule assigned the power to make it to the central government.
predicates.eviction_order_is_void: The eviction order is legally invalid and has no effect.

issues.definition: When a challenge to an eviction order establishes that an unempowered official issued it, the order is void.

issues.legal_issue: Findings on issues unnecessary to an appeal’s disposition on a threshold ground are not to be considered in pending or future proceedings between the parties.
material_facts: The High Court considered the occupants’ derivative title and other issues in reviewing the eviction direction.
The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal because the official who issued the direction lacked authority.
Some of the other issues were pending in separate proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s observations and conclusions on the other issues were not to be taken into consideration in proceedings pending or to be taken in the future.
issues.legal_principle: Where an appeal can be disposed of on a threshold ground, it is unnecessary to decide other issues, particularly issues that are sub judice in separate proceedings. The Court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this direction.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_judgment: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment deciding a writ petition.
predicates.appeal_resolved_on_threshold_ground: The appeal is disposed of on a ground that makes it unnecessary to resolve other issues.
predicates.lower_court_decided_unnecessary_issues: The lower court made findings on issues that were unnecessary to the appeal’s disposition, including issues pending in separate proceedings.
predicates.lower_court_other_issue_findings_not_con: The lower court’s findings on those other issues are not considered in pending or future related proceedings.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a writ judgment is resolved on a threshold ground and the lower court decided unnecessary issues, those findings are not considered in related proceedings.
